item.text: {"debateNumber":219,"decisions":[{"moveId":"expected-world-evidence-of-absence","label":"Appeal to authority","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The exact definition requires Stenger’s status to be used as though it settles the argument. Here the substantive move is an expectation-based inference: a God hypothesis should predict a certain world, and failed expectations could evidence absence. The assessment’s material criticism is that no expected condition, failure, discriminating prediction, or relevant God conception is specified. That establishes underdevelopment and weak warrant, not reliance on Stenger’s authority.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/appeal-to-authority/","context":"Shermer attributes to the physicist Victor Stenger the proposition that, if God existed, the world should exhibit certain conditions and that their absence would count against God."},{"moveId":"ultimate-beliefs-beyond-proof","label":"Special pleading","type":"fallacy","decision":"accepted","rationale":"The move places supposedly “greater” meaning-conferring beliefs beyond the proof applicable to “shallow truths,” thereby applying a different evidential standard to a favored class of commitments. No principled reason is supplied for making significance determine evidential status. The assessment identifies precisely this material defect: the division is neither defined nor defended, lacks an epistemic principle, and risks insulating Christian belief from scrutiny.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/special-pleading/","context":"McGrath distinguishes provable “shallow truths” from greater beliefs that provide meaning, purpose, and value, claiming that the latter ultimately lie beyond proof."},{"moveId":"scientific-theories-change","label":"Argument from ignorance","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"McGrath does not treat Christianity as true because it has not been disproved, nor current science as false because future conclusions are unknown. He uses historical revision to argue only for modesty about certainty. The assessment criticizes the failure to show present unreliability or increased probability for Christianity and notes mismatch with Shermer’s probabilistic standard. Those are relevance and warrant limitations, not truth inferred from ignorance.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/argument-from-ignorance/","context":"McGrath cites the replacement of an earlier cosmological consensus and observes that present speakers cannot know what scientific investigators will conclude a century later."},{"moveId":"scientific-theories-change","label":"Red herring","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Past scientific revision is directly related to the disputed confidence placed in present scientific judgments, so it does not materially divert attention to an unrelated substitute issue. The assessment says the example addresses certainty more directly than Shermer’s probabilistic position and leaves important burdens unmet, but it still credits the move as pertinent and responsive. Incomplete response contact is not the defined diversion required for a red herring.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/red-herring/","context":"In direct reply to confidence in current evidential judgments, McGrath contrasts an overturned cosmological consensus with uncertainty about scientific opinion one hundred years from now."},{"moveId":"many-gods-one-further","label":"Base-rate neglect","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The move foregrounds an aggregate count of religions and gods rather than underweighting a general background rate in favor of a vivid local case. Its probability inference lacks evidence that the traditions are comparable, but no neglected prior or background frequency is identified. The assessment’s material criticism is that multiplicity alone does not determine comparative probabilities and that the formulation imposes unsupported symmetry. That is insufficient warrant, not base-rate neglect.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/base-rate-neglect/","context":"Shermer invokes thousands of religions and many mutually rejected gods, asking how probable it is that Yahweh alone is true and describing skepticism as going “one God further.”"},{"moveId":"science-and-faith-enrich","label":"Subjective validation","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The excerpt reports a subjective effect—faith enriched McGrath’s understanding of science—and the locked proposition is limited to that enrichment and noncompetition. It does not clearly infer that Christianity is externally accurate because the experience resonated personally. The assessment distinguishes usefulness from truth but expressly says the motion-level truth inference remains unstated and incomplete. Missing independent evidence cannot substitute for the definition’s required validation inference.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/subjective-validation/","context":"McGrath describes his realization that faith gave science new significance and enriched his vision of scientific inquiry, presenting science and faith as complementary rather than competitive."},{"moveId":"recurring-resurrection-myths","label":"Appeal to authority","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Joseph Campbell is offered as a shorthand illustration of comparative myth analysis, not as an authority whose status establishes recurrence, diffusion, or independent creation. Shermer also supplies a substantive historical example and proposed mechanisms, however thinly supported. The assessment’s material defects are absent corroboration, undefined similarities, lack of comparative controls, and failure to establish equivalence or derivation. None is reliance on Campbell’s status as dispositive.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/appeal-to-authority/","context":"Shermer cites a purported pre-Christian resurrection narrative, recurring mythic themes, diffusion or simultaneous creation, and invites listeners to think of a Joseph Campbell-style deconstruction."},{"moveId":"comparative-worldviews-break-bubble","label":"Base-rate neglect","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Shermer focuses on encounters with equally committed believers, but the record identifies no general background rate or prior probability that he underweights. The assessment instead finds that equal commitment does not establish equal warrant and that the traditions’ actual evidence remains unexamined. That is an unsupported comparative inference from salient cases, but it does not materially instantiate the exact base-rate-neglect definition without an identifiable neglected base rate.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/base-rate-neglect/","context":"Shermer recounts meeting adherents of unfamiliar worldviews who were as committed as he had been to Christianity, leading him to reinterpret his former certainty as socially situated belief."},{"moveId":"comparative-worldviews-break-bubble","label":"Subjective validation","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Although autobiographical, the move appeals to the observable plurality of equally committed communities rather than treating a proposition as accurate because it feels privately resonant. Shermer’s changed confidence is the result being described, not the validating premise defined by this bias. The assessment materially criticizes the jump from equal commitment to equal warrant or broad falsity and the lack of evidential comparison; it does not diagnose truth being inferred from personal resonance.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/subjective-validation/","context":"Shermer describes how direct encounters with confident adherents of alternative meaning-giving worldviews caused him to regard his own inherited Christianity as personally held rather than uniquely true."},{"moveId":"ungrounded-values-reflect-society","label":"Special pleading","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The move challenges socially generated values as potentially reproducing prejudice, but it does not articulate a common standard and then exempt Christianity from it. The assessment notes that McGrath has not shown why reflection, evidence, or shared interests cannot correct secular values and has not explained how Christianity avoids parallel distortions. Those unmet comparative burdens make the argument underdeveloped; they do not establish that an unprincipled exception is actually applied within this move.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/special-pleading/","context":"McGrath suggests that meaning and value without an external basis may amount to elevating a society’s prejudices, and he asks what such commitments can be based upon."},{"moveId":"secular-values-risk-projection","label":"Special pleading","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"McGrath argues that naturalistically generated values may project desired preferences as self-evident, but this move does not expressly apply that evidential standard to secular morality while granting Christianity an exception. The assessment says possibility does not establish secular instability and that transcendent grounding has not been shown available or less projective. This is an unfulfilled burden and weak evidence, not a materially instantiated differential standard.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/special-pleading/","context":"McGrath separates a naturalistic genealogy of values from objective justification, warning that people can elevate what they want to be true into supposedly self-evident moral principles."},{"moveId":"meaning-available-without-religion","label":"Subjective validation","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Personal or experiential meaningfulness is relevant evidence for the limited proposition that people can experience meaning without religion; the move does not clearly use that experience to prove an external worldview true. The assessment carefully distinguishes psychological availability from philosophical adequacy and objective grounding. Its material criticism is that Shermer has not shown the naturalistic account meets the stronger grounding standard, not that he validates external truth through private resonance.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/subjective-validation/","context":"Shermer says scientific understanding can be deeply existentially meaningful and that purpose, meaning, and love are available in both religious and nonreligious lives."},{"moveId":"science-does-not-answer-why","label":"Argument from ignorance","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The move identifies a question McGrath believes science does not answer, but it does not conclude that Christianity’s answer is therefore true or that naturalism is false merely for lack of proof. The assessment explicitly treats positive theistic support as absent: identifying science’s boundary establishes neither that an external answer exists nor that Christianity supplies a warranted one. Such a missing inference is underdevelopment, not an instantiated argument from ignorance.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/argument-from-ignorance/","context":"McGrath distinguishes science’s account of how human beings arose from the existential question of why humans are here and urges that the language of “why” remain open."},{"moveId":"science-does-not-answer-why","label":"Equivocation","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The word “why” is insufficiently specified and could concern cause, purpose, or desired significance, but the excerpt does not demonstrably begin with one meaning and shift to another to strengthen a conclusion. The assessment calls the term ambiguous and requires McGrath to specify the explanatory target. Ambiguity alone, without a material meaning shift in the reasoning, does not satisfy the exact definition of equivocation.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/equivocation/","context":"McGrath contrasts scientific explanations of how humanity came to exist with the allegedly distinct and important question of why humanity is here."},{"moveId":"christianity-confronts-suffering-tension","label":"Red herring","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The passing comparison to atheism does not replace or conceal Christianity’s suffering problem; McGrath immediately identifies suffering as Christianity’s own tension and calls the objection legitimate. The assessment emphasizes this direct concession and exceptional contact with the central challenge. Its material limitation is that acknowledgment does not yet reconcile suffering with divine power and compassion, which is an incomplete defense rather than diversion from the disputed issue.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/red-herring/","context":"McGrath briefly notes that worldviews have points of tension, mentions widespread belief as a possible tension for atheism, and then expressly concedes suffering as Christianity’s legitimate tension with reality."},{"moveId":"selective-credit-defies-falsification","label":"Special pleading","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The asymmetric favorable-outcome rule described by Shermer would satisfy special pleading if it were being used by the speaker under assessment. Here, however, Shermer’s move criticizes believers for allegedly crediting God for good results while exempting God from bad ones. The assessment’s own limitation is Shermer’s insufficient demonstration that McGrath actually applies this rule. Tagging Shermer’s diagnostic move would improperly assign it the defect it attacks rather than a defect in its own reasoning.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/special-pleading/","context":"Shermer argues that some believers credit God when outcomes are favorable, withhold blame when outcomes are unfavorable, and thereby make divine intervention compatible with every possible result."},{"moveId":"selective-credit-defies-falsification","label":"Confirmation bias","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Selectively counting good outcomes and discounting bad ones is confirmation bias in the belief practice Shermer describes, but the candidate must assess Shermer’s move itself. Shermer is exposing, not performing, that selective interpretation. The assessment materially questions whether he has shown that McGrath’s actual framework uses the alleged pattern and whether theological distinctions are independently unprincipled. It does not show Shermer seeking or interpreting evidence to preserve his own prior view in the defined manner.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/confirmation-bias/","context":"Shermer presents favorable divine credit and unfavorable divine exemption as an unfalsifiable pattern in prayer and providential interpretation, asking what observation could ever count against the belief."},{"moveId":"faith-motivates-relief","label":"Red herring","type":"fallacy","decision":"accepted","rationale":"In response to suffering’s evidential challenge to an omnipotent and compassionate God, McGrath redirects attention to the related practical fact that Christianity condemns suffering and motivates believers to relieve it. That may establish an ethical benefit, but it leaves the original divine-permission and intervention challenge unanswered. The assessment makes this material: responsiveness is particularly weak, human relief does not answer Shermer’s inference, and practical fruit is not evidence of theological truth.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/red-herring/","context":"After conceding suffering as a legitimate Christian problem, McGrath emphasizes that Christians regard suffering as wrong and enter relief work or medicine to improve the world within human limits."},{"moveId":"jesus-claimed-historically-reliable","label":"Subjective validation","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"McGrath states both personal belief in historical reliability and a sense of deep significance, but he does not clearly say that the story is historically reliable because it feels significant to him. Indeed, he concedes he cannot prove the claim. The assessment’s material defect is that historical reliability is asserted without evidence and alternatives are not compared. Mere first-person commitment and missing support do not establish the defined inference from private resonance to accuracy.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/subjective-validation/","context":"McGrath says he believes the Jesus story is historically reliable, explicitly acknowledges that he cannot prove it, and adds that he finds something deeply significant in it."},{"moveId":"old-resurrection-story-insulated","label":"Argument from ignorance","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Shermer asks how the resurrection is known and alleges that antiquity permits theological insulation, but he does not explicitly infer that the resurrection is false solely because it has not been proved. The assessment credits the epistemic challenge while criticizing his failure to examine historical arguments, identify insulating mechanisms, or show that age discredits testimony. Those are evidential and charitable limitations, not the exact ignorance inference required by the catalog.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/argument-from-ignorance/","context":"Shermer characterizes the Christian resurrection story as old enough to be lost in time and buried behind theology, then presses the question of how anyone knows it occurred."},{"moveId":"sentient-flourishing-moral-standard","label":"Appeal to authority","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Bentham’s name accompanies a substantive consideration—sentient beings’ capacity to suffer—rather than replacing the reasoning with his status. Shermer independently states survival, flourishing, and reduced suffering as the proposed moral baseline. The assessment’s material limitations concern the missing normative bridge and unresolved measurement and tradeoffs among individuals and species. It does not criticize reliance on Bentham’s authority as settling the standard.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/appeal-to-authority/","context":"Shermer proposes sentient survival, flourishing, and suffering as a naturalistic moral starting point and quotes Jeremy Bentham’s question about whether beings can suffer."},{"moveId":"morality-needs-beyond-us-framework","label":"Begging the question","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"McGrath asserts that morality needs a framework beyond individual preference and offers Christianity as a candidate source, but the excerpt does not derive that conclusion from premises that already assume it. The assessment identifies an unsupported necessity claim, absent evidence, and failure to show Christianity true, unique, or objective. An undefended premise may be weak, but without a circular structure it does not meet the exact definition of begging the question.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/begging-the-question/","context":"McGrath says a moral framework beyond us is needed to answer the grounding question and adds that, from a Christian perspective, human beings possess enormous importance."},{"moveId":"faith-motivates-good-closing","label":"Belief bias","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The move improperly connects a desirable motivational effect with validity, but the record does not present a separate argument whose logical validity McGrath judges according to whether its conclusion feels believable. The assessment diagnoses the unsupported transition from usefulness to truth, not evaluation of inference form through a believable conclusion. Subjective validation captures that expressly personal transition more exactly, so accepting belief bias would duplicate the same defect without independently meeting its definition.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/belief-bias/","context":"McGrath closes by saying faith gives him a worldview and desire to improve the world, and that this is why he regards God as both an important and a valid idea."},{"moveId":"faith-motivates-good-closing","label":"Subjective validation","type":"bias","decision":"accepted","rationale":"McGrath expressly moves from what he personally finds in faith—a motivating worldview and desire to act—to the conclusion that God is a valid idea. This treats personal resonance and practical usefulness as support for validity beyond merely reporting subjective importance. The assessment identifies exactly this material defect: motivational benefit does not establish accuracy, no independent evidence is supplied, and the transition from personal experience to reality beyond imagination remains unsupported.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/subjective-validation/","context":"In his closing synthesis, McGrath repeatedly frames faith’s worldview and action-guiding motivation as what works “for me,” then uses that experience to call God an important and valid idea."}]}
